svg.title: WHAT A HUB SOLVES
svg.desc: Comparison of three district depots without a hub and one charging hub serving the same districts. One: three separate grid upgrades versus one shared upgrade. Two: districts pay the utility side upfront and wait for refunds, while at hub scale utilities often pay, 9 million dollars in Brooklyn and 2.7 MW in Oakland. Three: peak draw of about 10 kW per bus versus about 2 kW with managed charging, from New York City’s modelling. Four: chargers installed site by site versus in about four weeks above ground in Brooklyn. Five: districts buy their chargers versus a monthly fee to the operator, which owns the chargers (company-stated). The size of the saving is not published.
svg.text: The same three districts, without a hub
and with one. Five things it changes.
WITHOUT A HUB · EACH DISTRICT ON ITS OWN
WITH A HUB · ONE BUS COMPANY’S YARD

g.text: The size of the saving is not published.
First, one grid upgrade instead of many.
Without a hub, every depot needs its own. A
hub needs one, shared by many fleets.
Second, scale gets the utility to pay: nine
million dollars in Brooklyn. A small
district depot usually pays upfront and
Third, more buses per kilowatt. New York
City’s study estimated managed charging cuts
the peak from about ten kilowatts to two per
Fourth, faster chargers. In Brooklyn they
went in above ground in about four weeks, in
modules that grow with the contracts.
Fifth, districts pay nothing upfront. The
operator owns the chargers and can bill a
The size of the saving is not published.
